evidence.description: GDB at print_board+0x33c (49th call, round_idx=48) confirms format1 at buf+0x1000 contains bytes 0x25 0x6e ('%n') followed by 'AAAAAAAAA|R04W00|\n'. buf[0:8] = 0x4141414141414141 (8 A's from accumulated content).

Program exits normally (rc=0, 'Bye bye!') with %n in format1. No SIGSEGV observed. This suggests either: (1) %n is not executed because format1 is re-initialized at start of each print_board call and the corrupted format1 is only present during the loop where it may not be reached by a sprintf call, or (2) %n executes but writes 0 to *buf=0x4141414141414141 which somehow does not crash (unlikely). The exact execution path of %n within the loop requires further GDB tracing.

verification_result.details: GDB confirms %n (0x25 0x6e) is present in corrupted format1 at buf+0x1000 after overflow with guess='AAAAAAAAAAAAAAA%nAAAAAAAAA'. buf[0:8] = 0x4141414141414141. However, program exits normally (rc=0) without SIGSEGV. The %n execution within the loop-internal sprintf could not be dynamically confirmed via GDB breakpoint due to breakpoint timing issues. The primitive remains CANDIDATE: %n is confirmed in format1, but its execution and memory write effect are not dynamically verified.

primitives.notes: ARB_WRITE via %n is CANDIDATE, not VERIFIED, because: (1) %n is confirmed in corrupted format1 via GDB, (2) buf[0:8] is confirmed as attacker-controlled (0x4141414141414141), (3) but no crash or memory modification was observed, suggesting %n may not be executed by a loop-internal sprintf before the loop exits. The format1 is re-initialized at the start of each print_board call, so the corrupted format1 only exists transiently during the loop where overflow occurs. Further GDB tracing with precise breakpoint placement on the loop-internal border sprintf (0x1aaf) after format1 corruption would be needed to confirm %n execution. The write value would be 0 (bytes written before %n as first specifier), and the write target would be *buf (attacker-controlled first 8 bytes of accumulated content).

non_primitives.reason: RIP_CONTROL is not achievable because the overflow feedback loop (format1 corruption removing %s) prevents the overflow from reaching the return address at rbp+0x8 (buf+0x1098). The canary at rbp-0x8 (buf+0x1088) is also not corrupted. Without canary corruption or return address overwrite, RIP_CONTROL is not possible through this BUG alone.

STACK_CONTROL (canary corruption/stack pivot) is not achievable because the overflow feedback loop prevents content from reaching the canary at buf+0x1088. The maximum overflow reaches buf+0x1000 (format1) but does not progress further due to the feedback loop.

source.root_cause: In print_board, the content buffer at [rbp-0x1090] (4096 bytes) is NOT initialized before the first sprintf call. The first sprintf uses buf as the first %s argument (sprintf(buf, format1, buf, pad_buf)), which reads the uninitialized stack memory via %s until a NUL byte is found. On the very first call to print_board (when round_idx=0), there is no previous buf[0]=0x00 to terminate the %s read, so residual stack data from prior function calls (fopen, setvbuf, read_int, generate_tokenset, generate_answer, init_game) is read and incorporated into the output buffer, then printed to stdout via printf('\n%s\n', buf).
source.description: Uninitialized stack memory read via self-referential sprintf(buf, fmt, buf, ...) on first print_board call. The buffer at [rbp-0x1090] is not zeroed before first use. The first sprintf reads buf via %s, picking up 3 bytes of residual stack data (0x60 0xec 0x1f = value 0x1fec60) before hitting a NUL byte at buf[3]. This data is printed to stdout in the first print_board output, appearing between the initial newline and the border line '----'.

chain: Uninitialized stack buffer at [rbp-0x1090] in print_board (no memset/zeroing before first use)
First sprintf(buf, format1, buf, pad_buf) reads buf via %s on uninitialized memory
Residual stack data (3 bytes: 0x60 0xec 0x1f) read until NUL at buf[3]
Leaked data incorporated into output buffer and printed via printf('\n%s\n', buf)

controlled_element.what: Uninitialized stack memory content (residual data from prior function calls)
controlled_element.how: The attacker triggers the first print_board call by completing the init phase (providing gameboard_size and letting init() run). The first call to play() -> print_board() reads uninitialized stack memory via the self-referential sprintf(buf, fmt, buf, ...) pattern. The attacker does not control WHAT data is leaked (it depends on prior stack usage), but controls WHEN the leak occurs (by completing init to reach the first play iteration).

preconditions.description: The program must reach the first call to print_board. This requires completing the init phase: providing a valid gameboard_size (1-26) via read_int, which triggers fopen(/dev/urandom), generate_tokenset, generate_answer, and init_game. After init returns, main calls play(), which calls print_board() at the start of the first iteration.
preconditions.necessity: Without reaching print_board, the uninitialized read cannot occur. The init phase must complete successfully (valid size, successful fopen, successful mallocs).

preconditions.description: The print_board buffer at [rbp-0x1090] must NOT be initialized before the first sprintf call. This is always true: the code does not call memset or zero the buffer before the first sprintf. The only zeroing happens AFTER the printf output (mov BYTE PTR [rbp-0x1090], 0x0 at 0x1ae8), which sets buf[0]=0x00 for subsequent calls but does not affect the first call.
preconditions.necessity: If the buffer were zeroed before first use, the %s read would find buf[0]=0x00 immediately and read 0 bytes, preventing the leak.

preconditions.description: The residual stack data at buf[0] must not be 0x00 (NUL). If buf[0] happened to be 0x00 from prior stack usage, the %s read would terminate immediately and no data would be leaked. In practice, buf[0..2] contains 0x60 0xec 0x1f (value 0x1fec60) from prior fopen/setvbuf internal operations, with the first NUL at buf[3].
preconditions.necessity: If the first byte were NUL, the leak would produce 0 bytes. The actual residual data has a non-NUL first byte, enabling the 3-byte leak.

preconditions.description: This is the FIRST call to print_board. On subsequent calls, buf[0] is set to 0x00 (at 0x1ae8 after the printf), so the %s read finds NUL immediately and reads 0 bytes. The leak only occurs on the first call.
preconditions.necessity: The leak is specific to the first print_board invocation. Subsequent calls do not leak because buf[0]=0x00 persists (stack frame is reused).

alias_key_findings.alias: buf is BOTH the destination (rdi) AND the first %s source argument (rdx). This self-referential pattern means the existing buf content is read via %s and appended to by the sprintf output. On the first call, buf is uninitialized, so %s reads residual stack data.
alias_key_findings.implication: The self-referential sprintf pattern is the mechanism that causes the uninitialized read. The %s format specifier reads from buf (uninitialized) until NUL, and the result is written back to buf, incorporating the leaked data into the output.

alias_key_findings.alias: The first NUL byte in the uninitialized buffer is at offset 3. The 3 bytes before it (0x60 0xec 0x1f) are residual stack data from prior function calls (fopen/setvbuf internal operations).
alias_key_findings.implication: The leak is limited to 3 bytes because the first NUL in the uninitialized buffer is at offset 3. The leaked value 0x1fec60 is a small integer/offset, NOT a full pointer, NOT the canary (canary=0xc00000000), NOT a heap/libc/stack address.

alias_key_findings.alias: After the final printf('\n%s\n', buf), the code executes 'mov BYTE PTR [rbp-0x1090], 0x0' which sets buf[0]=0x00. This persists for subsequent print_board calls because the stack frame is reused.
alias_key_findings.implication: The leak only occurs on the FIRST print_board call. On subsequent calls, buf[0]=0x00 causes the %s read to terminate immediately (0 bytes read), preventing further leaks.

mitigations.name: PIE / ASLR
mitigations.primitive_impact: The leaked value 0x1fec60 is a small integer/offset (3 bytes), NOT a full pointer. It does not directly leak the PIE base, heap base, or libc base. However, it does demonstrate that uninitialized stack data can be read and output, which in principle could leak more sensitive values if the stack residue contained pointers. The 3-byte leak is limited by the NUL at buf[3].

mitigations.name: Stack Canary
mitigations.primitive_impact: The canary (0xc00000000) is stored at [rbp-0x8], which is far from the buffer at [rbp-0x1090] (offset 0x1088 = 4232 bytes). The uninitialized read only reaches buf[3] (first NUL), so the canary is NOT leaked. The canary does not prevent the info leak itself (it only protects against stack buffer overflows).

mitigations.name: NX
mitigations.primitive_impact: NX does not affect the INFO_LEAK primitive. NX prevents code execution on the stack, but the leak is a read operation, not an execution attempt.

mitigations.name: Partial RELRO
mitigations.primitive_impact: RELRO does not affect the INFO_LEAK primitive. RELRO protects GOT entries from being overwritten, which is irrelevant to an uninitialized memory read.

evidence.description: Stack allocation 'sub rsp, 0x10a0' allocates 4256 bytes. Buffer at [rbp-0x1090], content area is 0x1000=4096 bytes. No memset or zeroing of the content area before first use.

First sprintf call: sprintf(buf, format1, buf, pad_buf). rdi=buf (dest at rbp-0x1090), rdx=buf (first %s source). buf is BOTH destination and first %s argument, causing content accumulation. On first call, buf is uninitialized, so %s reads residual stack data.

After printf output: 'mov BYTE PTR [rbp-0x1090], 0x0' sets buf[0]=0x00. This persists for subsequent calls (stack frame reused), preventing the uninitialized read on later calls. This confirms the leak is specific to the first call.

gdb observation at print_board entry (first call): buf[0..7] = 0x60 0xec 0x1f 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00 0x00. The first 3 bytes (0x60 0xec 0x1f = value 0x1fec60) are non-NUL residual stack data. First NUL at buf[3]. The first sprintf reads these 3 bytes via %s before hitting NUL.

Program output (first print_board call): '
`\xec\x1f--------------------
|Round|Input|Reward|
--------------------

[0] Guess'. The 3 bytes 0x60 0xec 0x1f appear between the initial newline and the border line '----' in the output. These bytes are NOT attacker-provided (only gameboard_size '5' was sent) and NOT part of the fixed format strings.
Second print_board call output: no leaked bytes between newline and border line. Confirms buf[0]=0x00 (set at 0x1ae8 after first call) prevents the uninitialized read on subsequent calls.

Reproducibility: 3 independent runs all leaked the same 3 bytes (0x60 0xec 0x1f = value 0x1fec60). The leak is deterministic because the same code path (init -> play -> print_board) produces the same stack residue.

Leaked value analysis: 0x1fec60 is a small integer/offset, NOT a full pointer. It is NOT the canary (canary=0xc00000000), NOT a heap address (heap=0x555555559000+), NOT a libc address (libc=0x7ffff7da3000+), NOT a stack address (stack=0x7ffffffde000+). It is residual internal data from fopen/setvbuf library operations.

primitives.notes: BUG-002 produces a VERIFIED INFO_LEAK primitive. The leak is DIRECT (no intermediate object reuse or metadata manipulation required). The uninitialized stack buffer at [rbp-0x1090] in print_board is read via the self-referential sprintf(buf, fmt, buf, ...) pattern on the first call, leaking 3 bytes of residual stack data (0x1fec60) to stdout. The leak is limited in scope: only 3 bytes are leaked (first NUL at buf[3]), and the leaked value is a small integer/offset rather than a sensitive pointer. The leak only occurs on the first print_board call; subsequent calls have buf[0]=0x00 preventing further leaks. The leaked data does not directly compromise ASLR (no full pointer leaked) or the canary (canary is at a different stack location). However, the primitive demonstrates that uninitialized stack memory can be read and output, which could be more dangerous if the stack residue contained sensitive pointers in a different execution context. The primitive is classified as INFO_LEAK (not ARB_READ) because the attacker does not control the read address — the read target is fixed at the stack buffer location, and the data read depends on prior stack usage rather than attacker-controlled addressing.

non_primitives.reason: The uninitialized read does not qualify as ARB_READ because the attacker does not control the read address. The read target is always the fixed stack buffer at [rbp-0x1090] in print_board. The attacker cannot specify an arbitrary address Y to read from. The data read is residual stack content, not data at an attacker-chosen address. This is classified as INFO_LEAK (uninitialized memory read) rather than ARB_READ.

While the read occurs at a fixed stack offset, it is not a relative/OOB read in the traditional sense. The buffer is not being indexed out of bounds — the sprintf %s simply reads from the start of the uninitialized buffer until NUL. There is no index manipulation or bounds bypass. The issue is purely the lack of initialization, not an out-of-bounds access. Classified as INFO_LEAK (uninitialized memory) rather than RELATIVE_READ.
